prompt: Some people believe high schools should require all students to wear a school uniform. Others believe students should be free to choose their own clothing every day. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Some schools want every student in the same uniform, but I disagree with that idea. Students should be free to choose their own clothing. Picking your own outfit lets you express who you are, uniforms often do not save families money the way people assume, and forcing everyone into the same clothes does not actually fix the problems uniforms are supposed to solve. For these reasons, high schools should not require uniforms.

The first reason is that clothing is one of the few ways teenagers get to show their personality at school. A student who loves skateboarding might wear band shirts and skate brand hoodies, while a student who is into fashion might spend time putting together an outfit that says something about their interests. This small daily choice sounds minor, but it builds a sense of identity at an age when a lot of other decisions, like what classes to take or what time to wake up, are already made for you. Taking away clothing choice does not make school fairer, it just removes one normal part of being a teenager.

The second reason is that uniforms are often pitched as a way to save families money, but the opposite can be true. Uniform pieces from an approved supplier are usually more expensive per item than a plain t-shirt and jeans from a regular store, and families still have to buy regular clothes for weekends and after school, on top of the uniform. Instead of one clothing budget, families end up paying for two.

The third reason is that uniforms do not actually solve the problem they are supposed to solve. A school near my neighbourhood switched to uniforms hoping to reduce teasing about appearance, but students just started teasing each other about shoes, backpacks, and haircuts instead. The real issue is how students treat each other, and that has to be fixed through conversations and school programs, not a dress code.

For all of these reasons, I believe students should keep the freedom to choose their own clothing. It supports self-expression, it does not guarantee any real savings, and it does not fix the behaviour problems it claims to solve. Schools should spend their energy on building a respectful environment instead of controlling what students wear.
weak_paragraph_example: Uniforms are a bad idea for schools. A lot of people do not like them and think they are annoying. Clothes are important to people and uniforms take that away. It is just not a good system and schools should think about that. There are probably other ways to handle it that would work better for everyone involved in the school.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for lacking specific supporting details. Phrases like a lot of people and other ways never name a real example, so the reader cannot picture anything concrete backing up the opinion.

prompt: Some people believe teachers give students too much homework and that daily homework should be significantly reduced. Others believe regular homework is necessary for students to succeed. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Teachers often assign homework in every subject every night, and I agree that daily homework should be significantly reduced. Too much homework leaves students exhausted, it does not actually improve learning the way people assume, and it takes away time students need for other important parts of life. For these reasons, schools should cut back on how much homework they assign.

The first reason is that heavy homework loads leave students running on too little sleep. When a student has an hour of math homework, an essay for English, and a chapter to read for science all due the next day, something has to give, and it is usually sleep. A tired student who shows up to first period after finishing homework at midnight is not going to focus well in class, which means the homework meant to help them ends up hurting their ability to learn the next day's lesson.

The second reason is that piling on homework does not automatically lead to better understanding. Research on this topic has found that after a certain point, extra practice questions stop helping and just become busywork. A student who already understands how to solve a type of math problem does not need thirty repeated questions, they need maybe five to confirm they have it, and then time to move on. Assigning more just because it looks thorough on paper wastes hours without teaching anything new.

The third reason is that homework crowds out time students need for other things that matter, like part-time jobs, family responsibilities, and sleep itself. A student who works a shift after school to help pay for their own expenses, or who has to watch younger siblings while a parent works late, simply does not have three extra hours free every night. Reduced homework would let these students keep up in school without sacrificing responsibilities they cannot walk away from.

For all of these reasons, I believe homework should be reduced. It costs students sleep, it stops helping after a certain point, and it ignores the real responsibilities many students already carry outside of school. A lighter, more focused homework load would let students actually absorb what they learn instead of just surviving the night.
weak_paragraph_example: Homework is fine I guess. Some days it feels like too much and other days it is not that bad. Teachers probably need to give some homework so students practise. But also maybe less homework would be nice sometimes. It really depends on the class and the teacher and how the student feels about that subject that day.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for having no clear, consistent opinion. It drifts between homework being fine, too much, and needed, so a marker cannot state the writer's actual position in one sentence.

prompt: Some people believe high schools should start the school day later in the morning. Others believe the current early start time should stay the same. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Most high schools start class around eight in the morning, and I agree that start times should be pushed later. Teenagers are biologically wired to fall asleep and wake up later than younger kids or adults, a later start would improve focus and safety, and it would not actually cause the scheduling problems people worry about. For these reasons, high schools should shift their start times.

The first reason is that teenage sleep cycles genuinely shift later during adolescence. This is not just teens being lazy, it is a real change in the body's internal clock that makes it hard to fall asleep before eleven at night, even for students who want to sleep earlier. When a school forces a wake-up time of six thirty to catch an early bus, students are getting far less sleep than they need, no matter how disciplined they try to be about bedtime.

The second reason is that a later start would make students safer and more focused. A student who has had enough sleep reacts faster while driving to school, pays closer attention during a first period math lesson, and is less likely to make careless mistakes on a test. Schools that have already tried later start times, some in the United States, have reported fewer car accidents involving teen drivers and improved grades in early classes, which shows this is not just a comfortable idea but one with real results.

The third reason is that the common objection, that a later start would ruin bus schedules and after-school sports, is manageable with some planning. Schools could stagger elementary and high school start times differently than they do now, and sports practices could simply shift later in the afternoon instead of ending later at night. These are scheduling adjustments, not reasons to keep students chronically underslept.

For all of these reasons, I believe high schools should start later in the morning. It respects how teenage bodies actually work, it improves safety and academic performance, and the logistical concerns can be solved without giving up the change entirely. A later bell would help students show up to class actually ready to learn.
weak_paragraph_example: Starting school later would be good. Students would like it a lot. It would probably help with grades and other stuff too. Buses would need to change I think but that is not really a huge deal in the end since schools change things all the time anyway for different reasons.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for vague, unsupported details. Claims like it would probably help with grades and other stuff never name a specific example or explanation, so there is nothing concrete a marker can credit.

prompt: Some people believe high schools should switch from letter grades to a pass or fail system. Others believe letter grades should stay because they show performance more clearly. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Some people want high schools to drop letter grades for a simple pass or fail system, but I disagree. Letter grades should stay because they give useful detail, they motivate students to aim higher than the minimum, and they matter for real decisions students make after high school. For these reasons, schools should keep the current grading system.

The first reason is that letter grades give far more useful information than a pass or fail label ever could. A student who earns an eighty five in chemistry clearly understands the material well, while a student who barely passes with a fifty one has real gaps that need attention, even though both students would show up as an identical pass under a pass or fail system. Teachers, students, and parents lose the ability to tell the difference between solid understanding and a shaky one.

The second reason is that letter grades push students to aim for more than the bare minimum. If the only goal is to pass, a student who is capable of an eighty percent might stop putting in effort once they hit the fifty percent mark, since anything above that earns the exact same result on paper. Grades give students a reason to keep improving even after they have technically cleared the bar, which builds a stronger work ethic overall.

The third reason is that letter grades genuinely matter for decisions after high school. University and college programs use grade averages to decide who gets accepted into competitive programs, and some scholarships require a specific average to qualify. A pass or fail transcript would make it impossible for admissions offices to tell a strong applicant from a student who barely scraped by, which would actually make the system less fair, not more.

For all of these reasons, I believe letter grades should stay in high schools. They give clearer information, they encourage students to keep improving, and they support fair decisions for university and scholarship applications. Removing them would take away a tool that helps both students and the people who evaluate their work.
weak_paragraph_example: Grades are important for school. But also pass or fail sounds relaxing for students. Grades can be stressful for some people which is a real problem. Then again without grades how would anyone know who did well. It is a tough call honestly and both sides make sense when you think about it.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for having no clear, consistent opinion. The paragraph bounces between defending grades and favouring pass or fail without ever settling on a position the writer is arguing for.

prompt: Some people believe high schools should offer more elective courses and fewer required courses. Others believe a strong set of required courses is more important than giving students choice. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
High schools currently require most students to take a long list of core subjects, and I agree that schools should offer more electives instead of piling on required courses. Electives keep students engaged, they let students build skills tied to their actual interests, and a smaller set of required courses can still cover the essentials without crowding out everything else. For these reasons, schools should shift toward more elective choice.

The first reason is that electives keep students engaged in a way required courses often cannot. A student who is forced into a required course they have no interest in tends to do the minimum just to pass, while that same student in an elective they chose, like photography, culinary arts, or coding, often puts in extra effort because they actually care about the outcome. Engagement like that leads to real learning instead of just checking a box.

The second reason is that electives let students build skills connected to what they might actually do later. A student interested in business could take an entrepreneurship elective and learn how to build a basic business plan, a skill they would never touch in a required math or history course. This kind of early exposure can help a student figure out a career direction years before they would otherwise get the chance.

The third reason is that a smaller list of required courses can still teach the essentials without needing to dominate a student's schedule. Core skills like reading, writing, and basic math can be built into a handful of well-designed required courses rather than a long list that eats up every spare block. This would free up room for electives without sacrificing the foundational skills schools are supposed to guarantee.

For all of these reasons, I believe high schools should offer more electives and reduce the number of required courses. Electives boost engagement, connect learning to real interests, and a leaner set of requirements can still cover the basics. Giving students more choice would make high school feel less like a checklist and more like preparation for their actual future.
weak_paragraph_example: Electives are cool. Some kids like art and some like gym class. Required courses are also there for reasons. Schools have a lot to think about with schedules and stuff like that. It would be nice to have more choices probably but who knows how that would even work out in the end.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for vague, unsupported details. It never names a specific elective, skill, or example of why choice matters, leaving only general statements a marker cannot credit as real support.

prompt: Some people believe schools should shift to a longer school day paired with a shorter school year. Others believe the standard school calendar should stay the way it is. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Some people have proposed longer school days combined with a much shorter school year, but I disagree with that plan. The standard calendar should stay because it matches how attention and energy actually work over a day, it protects the summer jobs and programs many students depend on, and it avoids burning teachers out faster than they already are. For these reasons, schools should keep the current calendar structure.

The first reason is that longer days do not match how student attention actually works. A student who is focused during a normal six hour day tends to lose concentration well before the end of an extended eight or nine hour version, especially in the last block. Adding more hours does not add more real learning, it mostly adds more hours of tired students staring at a clock, which does not help anyone reach a lesson's actual goal.

The second reason is that a shorter summer would seriously disrupt the jobs and programs many students rely on. A lot of teenagers use the summer to work at a summer camp, a retail job, or a family business to save money for things like a car or post-secondary tuition. Employers plan their summer staffing around the current break, and shrinking it would force students to choose between finishing the school year and keeping a job they need.

The third reason is that longer days would push teachers toward burnout even faster than they already experience. Teachers already spend hours outside the school day grading, planning, and communicating with parents, and stretching the actual teaching day longer would eat into the limited time they have to recover and prepare properly. Exhausted teachers deliver weaker lessons, which would undo any benefit the extra classroom hours were supposed to create.

For all of these reasons, I believe the standard school calendar should stay in place. Longer days do not match real attention spans, they threaten summer jobs students depend on, and they would push teachers toward burnout. The current balance between school time and break time already works, and changing it would create new problems without solving an existing one.
weak_paragraph_example: Longer days might be okay for some students. Summer is also nice though for different reasons. Teachers work hard already which everyone knows. Changing school schedules is a big decision for a school board to make. There are pros and cons on both sides that people should think about carefully before doing anything.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for having no clear, consistent opinion. It lists both sides without ever stating which position the writer is actually taking, so no single opinion can be pulled from the paragraph.

prompt: Some people believe students should be allowed to retake a test to improve a poor grade. Others believe a test grade should stand as the final result with no retakes allowed. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Some teachers refuse to let students retake a test no matter what happened the first time, but I agree that students should be allowed to retake a test to improve a poor grade. Retakes reward real learning instead of a single bad day, they teach responsibility rather than letting students avoid it, and they better reflect what a student actually knows by the end of a unit. For these reasons, schools should allow test retakes.

The first reason is that a single test cannot always capture what a student truly understands. A student might fail a test because they were sick that week, dealing with a family emergency, or simply had a moment of panic that made them blank on material they actually knew. A retake gives that student a second, fairer chance to show their real understanding instead of being permanently judged by one rough day.

The second reason is that retakes actually build responsibility rather than removing it. A retake is not automatic. A student usually has to redo practice problems, attend extra help, or meet with the teacher to prove they have studied the material again before earning the chance to retest. That process teaches a student how to recover from a setback and improve through effort, which is a far more useful life skill than simply accepting a low mark and moving on.

The third reason is that a retake gives a more accurate final picture of what a student knows by the end of a unit. If the goal of a test is to measure understanding, then a grade earned after a student studied harder and closed their gaps reflects that understanding more honestly than a grade earned before they had fully learned the material. Locking in the first attempt values timing over actual knowledge.

For all of these reasons, I believe students should be allowed to retake tests. It accounts for bad days, it builds real responsibility through the extra work required, and it produces a grade that reflects true understanding. Refusing retakes punishes students for being human instead of helping them actually learn the material.
weak_paragraph_example: Retakes are good for students who need them. Some students do not need them because they always do well. Tests are stressful for a lot of people honestly. Teachers have different rules about this in different classes which can be confusing. It depends on the situation and the student and the class overall.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for disorganized ideas. It jumps between unrelated points about strong students, stress, and teacher rules without ever developing one reason with a specific supporting detail.

prompt: Some people believe high schools should replace final exams with ongoing assessment throughout the semester. Others believe final exams are still the fairest way to measure what a student has learned. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Many high schools still rely heavily on a single final exam at the end of a course, and I agree that ongoing assessment throughout the semester would be a fairer replacement. Ongoing assessment reduces the damage of one bad day, it measures long-term understanding rather than short-term memorization, and it lowers the extreme anxiety that comes with a single high-pressure test. For these reasons, schools should shift toward ongoing assessment.

The first reason is that a single final exam puts an unreasonable amount of weight on one moment in time. A student who understood the material well all semester could still underperform on exam day due to poor sleep, illness, or simple nerves, and that one result can drag down an otherwise strong grade. Ongoing assessment spreads the evaluation across many smaller moments, so one rough day cannot undo months of solid work.

The second reason is that ongoing assessment measures real, lasting understanding instead of short-term cramming. A student preparing for one big final exam often memorizes facts for a few days and forgets most of them shortly after, which does not actually reflect learning. Regular quizzes, projects, and assignments spread throughout the term force a student to keep engaging with the material consistently, which builds knowledge that actually sticks.

The third reason is that ongoing assessment reduces the extreme stress tied to a single final exam. Students often describe exam week as the most anxious period of the school year, staying up late trying to review months of material at once. Spreading assessment out means no single day carries make-or-break weight, which allows students to show what they know without the added burden of crushing exam-week pressure clouding their performance.

For all of these reasons, I believe ongoing assessment is a fairer approach than relying on final exams alone. It protects students from one bad day, it rewards real understanding over short-term memorization, and it reduces unnecessary stress. Schools that make this shift would end up with grades that actually reflect what students learned over the whole course.

Final exams have been around forever so changing them would be a big deal for schools. It is hard to say what the best system actually is in the end.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for having no clear, consistent opinion. Phrases like sounds better maybe and it is hard to say never commit to a position, so a marker cannot identify what the writer actually believes.

prompt: Some people believe the voting age should be lowered to sixteen. Others believe the voting age should stay at eighteen. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Some countries have already lowered their voting age to sixteen, and I agree that Canada should consider the same change. Sixteen-year-olds are directly affected by many political decisions, they are capable of understanding the issues at stake, and starting to vote earlier builds a lasting habit of civic participation. For these reasons, the voting age should be lowered to sixteen.

The first reason is that decisions made by governments directly affect sixteen-year-olds, even though they currently have no say in who makes those decisions. Policies about education funding, minimum wage for part-time jobs, and public transit fares all shape a sixteen-year-old's daily life just as much as an adult's. Someone old enough to hold a part-time job and pay income tax on those earnings is old enough to have a voice in who sets the rules around that job.

The second reason is that sixteen-year-olds are capable of understanding political issues when given the chance to learn about them. High school civics courses already cover how government works, and many students actively follow news about climate policy, housing, or social issues that matter to them. A student who can analyze an argument in an English class or explain cause and effect in a history essay has the reasoning skills needed to evaluate a political platform.

The third reason is that voting at sixteen would build a habit that carries into adulthood. Research on voter turnout has shown that people who vote in their first eligible election are far more likely to keep voting for the rest of their lives. Introducing sixteen-year-olds to voting while they are still in a stable routine at home and school, rather than during the busy transition of moving out or starting a job at eighteen, could raise long-term participation rates.

For all of these reasons, I believe the voting age should be lowered to sixteen. It gives a voice to people already affected by political decisions, it respects their ability to understand the issues, and it builds a lifelong voting habit. Lowering the age would strengthen democracy rather than weaken it.
weak_paragraph_example: Voting at sixteen would be interesting. Some sixteen year olds care about politics and some do not care at all really. Eighteen is also a normal age for a lot of things in life. It is a tricky topic because people have strong opinions about it either way you look at things.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for having no clear, consistent opinion. The paragraph presents both ages as reasonable without ever stating which one the writer actually supports.

prompt: Some people believe public transit should be free for teenagers. Others believe teenagers should pay the same transit fare as adults. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Many teenagers pay full or near-full transit fare just like adults, and I agree that public transit should be free for teenagers instead. Free transit would remove a real financial barrier for students, it would encourage healthier transportation habits, and it would support access to school, jobs, and extracurricular activities that many teens cannot afford to reach otherwise. For these reasons, cities should make transit free for teenagers.

The first reason is that transit fares create a real financial burden for teenagers who often have limited or no income. A student who takes the bus to school and then again to a part-time job after school can easily spend several dollars a day, which adds up to a significant monthly cost for someone earning minimum wage for a handful of shifts a week. Free transit would let that money go toward savings, school supplies, or family needs instead.

The second reason is that free transit would encourage teenagers to build the habit of using public transportation instead of relying on rides from parents or, eventually, driving alone. A student who gets used to taking the bus or subway during high school is more likely to continue using transit as an adult, which reduces traffic congestion and the environmental impact of extra cars on the road. Starting that habit early, while the cost barrier is removed, makes it more likely to stick.

The third reason is that free transit would open up access to opportunities many teenagers currently cannot reach. A student interested in a specialized program, a job across town, or an extracurricular activity at another school might skip it entirely because the transit cost adds up over weeks and months. Removing that cost would let students choose activities and opportunities based on what actually interests them, not on what happens to be walking distance from home.

For all of these reasons, I believe public transit should be free for teenagers. It removes a real financial burden, it builds long-term sustainable transportation habits, and it widens access to school and work opportunities. Making transit free would be a small cost for cities to cover compared to the benefit it would give to young people finding their way.

Some cities have different rules about fares for younger riders which is interesting. Transportation is important in general for getting places on time and stuff like that around a city.

prompt: Some people believe cities should enforce a strict evening curfew for anyone under eighteen. Others believe a government-enforced curfew unfairly restricts teenagers who are not doing anything wrong. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Some cities have discussed enforcing a strict evening curfew for anyone under eighteen, but I disagree with that idea. A blanket curfew unfairly punishes responsible teenagers, it ignores legitimate reasons teens are out at night, and it does not actually address the small number of incidents it is meant to prevent. For these reasons, cities should not enforce a strict teen curfew.

The first reason is that a curfew punishes the vast majority of responsible teenagers for the actions of a small minority. Most teenagers who are out after a certain hour are doing something completely ordinary, like walking home from a part-time shift, finishing a study session at a friend's house, or heading back from a sports practice that ran late. Treating every teenager as a suspect simply for being outside after dark ignores the reality that most are not causing any trouble at all.

The second reason is that a curfew ignores legitimate situations that keep teenagers out later than a set cutoff. A student working a closing shift at a restaurant, or one coming home from a late evening game or rehearsal, would technically break curfew through no fault of their own. Families with parents working night shifts might also depend on an older teenager to be out handling errands or picking up younger siblings, and a strict curfew would criminalize that kind of everyday family responsibility.

The third reason is that curfews have not been shown to reliably reduce the problems they are supposed to solve. Studies on curfew laws in various cities have found little clear evidence that they lower youth crime rates, since most serious incidents involving teenagers happen during the day, often connected to school, rather than late at night. A law that mainly restricts innocent teenagers while barely touching the actual problem is not solving anything.

For all of these reasons, I believe cities should not enforce a strict curfew for teenagers. It punishes responsible teens, it ignores legitimate reasons for being out late, and it does not meaningfully reduce the problems it claims to target. Instead of a blanket restriction, cities should focus on the specific situations that actually cause harm.
weak_paragraph_example: Curfews might help some cities I guess. Teenagers are out at night sometimes for different reasons. Crime is a real issue in a lot of places which is unfortunate. Rules like this exist in some places already so it is not a totally new idea for a city council to think about.
weak_paragraph_issue: This fails Topic Development for having no clear, consistent opinion. It floats the idea that curfews might help without ever stating whether the writer actually supports or opposes them.

prompt: Some people believe local libraries should stay open on Sundays. Others believe library budgets are better spent extending weekday hours instead of adding weekend days. Write an essay stating your opinion on this topic, then give reasons and details that explain and support your opinion.
model_essay_strong:
Many local libraries currently close on Sundays, and I agree that they should stay open that day instead of relying only on extended weekday hours. Sunday hours reach students and families who cannot use the library during the week, they provide a quiet study space during a genuinely busy time, and they make better use of a public resource that many neighbourhoods rely on. For these reasons, libraries should open on Sundays.

The first reason is that many students and working parents simply cannot get to the library on weekdays, even with extended hours. A student with after-school sports, a part-time job, and homework every weeknight might not have a single free weekday evening to visit, while a parent working full-time hours has the exact same problem. Sunday is often the one day these families actually have free time together, so closing the library that day removes the only real chance many people have to use it.

The second reason is that Sunday hours give students a quiet, reliable place to study before a busy school week starts. A student who wants to finish an essay or study for a Monday test but has a noisy house full of siblings or guests would benefit from somewhere calm to focus. Weekday evening extensions do not solve this problem, since those hours are usually already full of dinner, homework already assigned that day, and family routines.

The third reason is that opening on Sundays makes better overall use of a resource the public is already paying for through taxes. A library that sits locked and empty one full day a week is not serving the community it was built for, especially in neighbourhoods where the library is one of the few free public spaces available. Shifting to Sunday hours, even if it means slightly shorter weekday extensions, would spread access more evenly across the people who actually need it.

For all of these reasons, I believe libraries should stay open on Sundays. It reaches families who cannot come during the week, it gives students a quiet place to prepare for the week ahead, and it makes fuller use of a shared public resource. A library open on the one day many people are actually free serves the community far better than one that is not.

prompt: Some people believe cities should prioritize building more skate parks and youth centres over other public amenities. Others believe that money should go toward amenities that serve the whole community, like parks and pools. prompt: Some people believe teenagers should be allowed to work more hours per week during the school year. Others believe current limits on teen work hours should stay in place to protect school performance. Many high schools only require physical education for the first year or two, and I agree that gym class should remain mandatory through every grade instead. Ongoing physical activity supports both physical and mental health, mandatory gym class reaches students who would never choose activity on their own, and it teaches lifelong habits that matter well beyond high school. For these reasons, physical education should stay a required course in every grade.

The first reason is that regular physical activity supports both physical and mental health in ways that matter throughout the teenage years, not just in grade nine. The second reason is that mandatory gym class reaches students who would never choose to be active on their own if given the choice. The third reason is that ongoing physical education teaches habits that carry into adulthood, when structured activity becomes much harder to build from scratch. A student who continues learning about different sports, stretching, and basic fitness principles throughout high school leaves with a wider range of activities they know how to do and enjoy, compared to a student who stopped taking gym after one required year and never revisited physical activity again.

For all of these reasons, I believe physical education should remain mandatory through every grade of high school. When school budgets shrink, sports programs are often protected first while other clubs get cut, but I disagree with automatically prioritizing sports this way. Non-sport clubs serve just as many students with genuine interests, they often require far less money to run than sports programs do, and cutting them first assumes sports matter more without any real evidence to support that assumption. For these reasons, schools should protect all extracurricular activities equally when facing budget cuts, not just sports.

The first reason is that non-sport clubs, like debate, robotics, or drama, serve just as many students with just as genuine an interest as any sports team does. A student who spends hours after school building a robot for a competition or memorizing lines for a school play is putting in the same kind of dedication as an athlete practising free throws, and their activity deserves the same respect and support from the school's budget, not automatic dismissal.

The second reason is that many non-sport clubs actually cost far less to run than sports programs do. A debate club might need a small budget for transportation to a tournament, while a sports team often requires equipment, uniforms, referees, and facility maintenance that adds up to a much larger yearly cost. If anything, cutting a low-cost club to protect a much more expensive sports program does not even make sense from a purely financial standpoint.

The third reason is that automatically prioritizing sports assumes they matter more to students overall, without any real evidence to back that assumption up. Some schools have more students involved in clubs like music, robotics, or student government than in a specific sports team, yet the sports program still gets protected first purely out of habit or tradition, not because more students would actually be affected by cutting it.

For all of these reasons, I believe schools should protect all extracurricular activities equally during budget cuts, rather than automatically favouring sports. Non-sport clubs serve just as many dedicated students, they often cost less to run, and prioritizing sports by default is not backed by real evidence. A fair budget decision should look at actual student involvement and cost, not old assumptions about which activities matter most.

prompt: Some people believe schools should require every student to participate in an intramural sports program at least once during their time in high school. model_essay_strong:
Intramural sports are usually treated as a completely optional activity, but I agree that schools should require every student to participate at least once during high school. A one-time requirement exposes students to activities they might never try on their own, it builds social connections outside a student's usual friend group, and requiring it only once, rather than every year, keeps the policy reasonable rather than overwhelming. For these reasons, schools should require every student to try intramural sports at least once.

The first reason is that a one-time requirement exposes students to activities they would likely never choose to try on their own. A student who assumes they dislike all sports because they were never interested in a competitive school team might discover they actually enjoy a low-pressure intramural badminton league or a casual volleyball night, simply because they were required to give it a try at least once. Without that push, many students would go through all of high school never finding out.

The second reason is that intramural sports build social connections outside a student's usual friend group in a way regular classes often do not. Intramural teams are often mixed by grade or randomly assigned rather than sorted by existing friendships, which means a student ends up interacting with classmates they might never otherwise talk to. These casual, low-stakes interactions can lead to new friendships that would not have formed inside a normal classroom setting.

The third reason is that requiring participation only once, rather than every single year, keeps the policy reasonable instead of becoming a burden. Students who genuinely dislike sports would only need to fulfill the requirement one time, at whatever point fits their schedule best, rather than being forced into ongoing participation year after year. This makes the requirement about exposure and opportunity rather than about turning every student into a dedicated athlete.

For all of these reasons, I believe schools should require every student to try intramural sports at least once during high school. It introduces students to activities they might otherwise skip entirely, it builds connections outside their usual social circle, and a one-time requirement keeps the policy fair and manageable. A single small push could open up an activity some students end up genuinely enjoying.
